title: Use language and communication in occupational learning programmes

lessons.title: Managing your own learning
lessons.html:
Learning in an occupational programme

An occupational learning programme, such as a learnership in fruit packing, seed production or macadamia de-husking, combines theory in a training venue with practical learning in the workplace. At NQF level 3 you are expected to take more responsibility for your own learning: planning, finding information, reflecting and using feedback.

Understanding the programme

  • Read the learner guide and the list of unit standards or modules with their outcomes and assessment criteria.
  • Know your credits, the timeline and the dates of assessments.
  • Identify your facilitator, workplace mentor, assessor and moderator, and what each does.
  • Understand your rights, such as the right to appeal an assessment decision, and your responsibilities, such as attendance and producing your own work.

Setting learning goals

Set personal goals for each module using the SMART approach. Example: 'By the end of March I will be able to calibrate the nut sizing machine without help and explain each step to my mentor.'

Learning styles and strategies

People learn in different ways: by seeing, hearing, reading or doing. Use a mix of strategies:

  • Observe skilled workers and ask them to explain why they do things.
  • Practise under supervision and then independently.
  • Make summaries, mind maps or flash cards of key terms.
  • Teach a fellow learner; explaining something tests your understanding.
  • Link theory to practice: when you learn about moisture content, check how it is measured at your workplace.

Time management

Balancing work, study and family is difficult. Make a weekly study plan, use short regular sessions rather than last-minute cramming, and tell your mentor early if you are falling behind.

lessons.title: Accessing and using information for learning
lessons.html:
Finding the information you need

Sources of information

SourceExamples
Programme materialsLearner guide, workbook, handouts
Workplace documentsSOPs, specifications, quality manuals, safety data sheets, production records
PeopleFacilitator, mentor, supervisor, quality controller, experienced co-workers
External sourcesIndustry body guidelines, government publications, reliable websites, libraries

Evaluating information

Not all information is reliable. Ask:

  • Who wrote it, and are they an expert or official body?
  • Is it current? Check dates and versions.
  • Is it relevant to South African conditions and your workplace?
  • Does it agree with other reliable sources?

Information from social media or hearsay must be checked before you rely on it.

Note-making and summarising

When reading for an assignment, make notes in your own words. Record the source of each note so you can refer to it. Use headings that match the assessment questions. A summary should capture the main ideas briefly without copying sentences.

Avoiding plagiarism

Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own. In a portfolio of evidence it can lead to your work being rejected. Write answers in your own words, and when you use a quotation or a figure from a document, say where it comes from.

Understanding assessment questions

  • Identify / list: name items briefly.
  • Describe: give the features or steps.
  • Explain: give reasons, causes or how something works.
  • Compare: show similarities and differences.
  • Evaluate: judge strengths and weaknesses and give a conclusion.
  • Demonstrate: show by doing.

lessons.title: Communicating in learning and assessment
lessons.html:
Taking part actively

In the training room

  • Ask questions to clarify and to go deeper: 'Why is the drying temperature limited for seed?'
  • Contribute your workplace experience to discussions.
  • In group work, agree roles, listen to all members and share the workload fairly.
  • Present group findings clearly: introduce, give main points with examples, conclude.

In the workplace

Your mentor or supervisor guides your practical learning. Communicate regularly:

  • Agree what tasks you will practise and when.
  • Ask for demonstrations and then practise while being observed.
  • Keep a logbook of tasks done, dates and who observed you.
  • Ask for signed witness statements as evidence.

Preparing for assessment

Assessments may include written tasks, knowledge tests, practical observation, oral questioning and review of workplace evidence. To prepare:

  1. Review the assessment criteria so you know what the assessor is looking for.
  2. Organise your portfolio: index, completed tasks, evidence, signed declarations.
  3. Practise explaining what you do and why, as oral questions are common in practical assessments.
  4. Ask the assessor to clarify any instruction you do not understand.

Reflection and feedback

Reflection means thinking about what you learnt, what went well, what was difficult and what you will do differently. A short reflection after each module helps you improve. When you receive feedback from an assessor, read it carefully. If the result is 'not yet competent', agree a plan for re-assessment. If you believe the assessment was unfair, you may follow the appeal procedure.

Communication barriers

Language can be a barrier if materials are in a second language. Build vocabulary, ask for explanations, discuss in your home language with peers and then express the ideas in the assessment language. Facilitators should accommodate reasonable needs, such as reading support.

Key points

  • Understand your programme's outcomes, assessment criteria and roles of facilitator, mentor and assessor.
  • Set SMART learning goals and manage your time.
  • Use reliable, current sources and write in your own words to avoid plagiarism.
  • Know what instruction words such as explain, compare and evaluate require.
  • Keep workplace evidence and reflect on feedback to improve.
